title: Microservices & Back-End Architecture
requirement: Extensive back-end experience: Node.js, Python, Java, or C#, plus microservices architecture.

questions.question: What is a microservices architecture and how does it differ from a monolith?
questions.answer: Microservices split an app into small, independently deployable services, each owning a business capability and its data. A monolith ships as one unit. You gain independent scaling and team autonomy, and pay in latency, consistency and ops overhead.
questions.keyTakeaway: Trade deployment simplicity for independent scaling and team autonomy.

questions.question: When would you advise against microservices for a new product?
questions.answer: I'd say no when the domain is unstable, the team is small, or nothing needs independent scaling. Boundaries drawn too early are expensive to move. A well-modularized monolith can split later with the strangler fig, once there are several teams to justify the overhead.
questions.keyTakeaway: Start with a modular monolith; split on stable boundaries, not on hype.

questions.question: How do microservices communicate, and how do you choose between synchronous and asynchronous communication?
questions.answer: Sync calls, REST or gRPC, fit when the caller needs the answer now, like payment validation. An async broker fits state changes others react to, like order-placed, and it absorbs spikes. I prefer async when eventual consistency is fine, and keep sync chains shallow since latency compounds per hop.
questions.keyTakeaway: Request-response over RPC; state changes over the broker.

questions.question: What does database-per-service mean, and how do you keep data consistent without cross-service joins?
questions.answer: Each service owns its schema and is the only writer. Others read through APIs or event-fed local copies, never its tables. Cross-service writes are eventually consistent, using events and sagas. I denormalize on purpose.
questions.keyTakeaway: Own your data, share state through events, accept eventual consistency.

diagram.title: Cross-service consistency
diagram.condition: Does the write span more than one service?

questions.question: What role does an API gateway play in a microservices system?
questions.answer: It's the single entry point: it routes traffic, terminates TLS and auth, and handles rate limiting and logging once. It hides internal topology so clients stay stable. I keep business logic out, or it becomes a bottleneck.
questions.keyTakeaway: The gateway centralizes edge concerns; it must not accumulate business logic.

questions.question: How do you prevent one failing service from cascading failures through the system?
questions.answer: I layer timeouts, bounded retries with backoff and jitter, and circuit breakers that fail fast and probe before restoring traffic. I add fallbacks where a degraded answer beats an error, and test with chaos exercises.
questions.keyTakeaway: Fail fast with timeouts, backoff, and breakers; degrade instead of cascading.

questions.question: How would you incrementally migrate a monolith to microservices without a big-bang rewrite?
questions.answer: I'd use the strangler fig. Put a routing facade in front of the monolith, then move one bounded context at a time, starting with low-risk, high-value pieces. Each new service gets its own store. I keep both paths working and roll the route back when errors climb.
questions.keyTakeaway: Strangle the monolith one boundary at a time behind a routing facade.

questions.question: A user request spans five services and fails intermittently. How do you find the cause?
questions.answer: Distributed tracing, from day one. One trace id rides headers through every hop, so a single trace shows the path and per-span latency. I tie structured logs and RED metrics to the same id. Without correlation ids, intermittent cross-service failures are nearly undebuggable.
questions.keyTakeaway: Trace ids across every hop turn a five-service mystery into one timeline.

questions.question: How do you decide where to draw the boundaries when decomposing a system into services?
questions.answer: I decompose around business capabilities and bounded contexts, like orders, pricing and inventory, each with its own language and reasons to change. The test is whether it can release independently and own its data. If two services always ship together, they're one. I start coarse, since merging later is harder than splitting.
questions.keyTakeaway: Draw boundaries around business capabilities that can own their data and release independently.

diagram.title: Testing a candidate boundary
diagram.condition: Can this capability ship and scale on its own?

questions.question: What is the saga pattern and when does a system need one?
questions.answer: A saga runs a multi-service flow as local transactions, with compensating actions undoing earlier steps if a later one fails, like reserve stock, charge card, create shipment. I skip two-phase commit because it holds locks and one slow participant stalls everything. Compensation is a business action like a refund, so I model failure paths like the happy path.
questions.keyTakeaway: Run multi-service workflows as local transactions plus compensating actions, never two-phase commit.

questions.question: In a saga, how do you choose between orchestration and choreography?
questions.answer: In choreography services react to events with no coordinator. That's low coupling, good for short flows, but the workflow only exists implicitly, so nobody knows where an order is. An orchestrator owns the flow, tracks state and fires compensations, which makes long sagas observable. I choreograph simple reactions and orchestrate sequential steps and timeouts.
questions.keyTakeaway: Choreograph simple event reactions; orchestrate long flows that need visible state and compensation.

questions.question: How would you implement a screen that needs data from five different services?
questions.answer: Two options. API composition calls the services in parallel and merges in memory, simple but coupled to every source's uptime. A CQRS read model is a store fed by the owners' events and shaped for the screen. I use it for cross-service joins or tight latency, accepting seconds of lag and a rebuildable projection.
questions.keyTakeaway: Compose small queries in parallel; build event-fed read models when you must join across services.

questions.question: How do you keep a provider service from breaking its consumers when it ships a change?
questions.answer: Consumer-driven contract testing. Each consumer publishes the requests it makes and the fields it needs, and the provider's pipeline verifies against all contracts before merge. The provider hears about breakage in minutes from CI, not in production, and unused fields become safe to delete. A schema registry extends it to events.
questions.keyTakeaway: Consumers publish contracts and every provider build verifies them, catching breaks before merge.

questions.question: How can retries make an outage worse, and how do you design them so they do not?
questions.answer: When a dependency slows, every caller retries and the load multiplies on the struggling service. I cap retries at one layer, not every hop, retry only idempotent operations, and use exponential backoff with full jitter. A retry budget as a percent of normal traffic and breakers keep it bounded.
questions.keyTakeaway: Bound retries with jitter and budgets, or synchronized retries will amplify the outage they fight.

questions.question: How do you evolve a service's API or events without breaking the services that depend on it?
questions.answer: My default is backward-compatible change: add optional fields, never rename or repurpose one, since an unseen consumer probably reads it. For REST I version only on a real break and run old and new side by side. For events, a schema registry rejects incompatible changes at publish. I delete deprecated paths when traffic hits zero.
questions.keyTakeaway: Make only backward-compatible changes by default; deprecate with telemetry, delete at zero traffic.

no.label: Version and dual-run
no.note: deprecate old once traffic hits zero

questions.question: How do you diagnose a service that passes its health checks but still serves errors to users?
questions.answer: I separate the probes. Liveness checks only the process, otherwise a DB blip becomes a restart storm. Readiness asks whether the instance can take traffic, and a failing one drains rather than gets killed. The classic lie is a health endpoint that always returns 200 while the connection pool is dead, so I verify with synthetic requests.
questions.keyTakeaway: Liveness restarts the process, readiness gates traffic; a lying 200 routes users to a dead instance.

questions.question: When a broker redelivers messages after a consumer crash, how do you stop duplicates from corrupting state?
questions.answer: I assume at-least-once delivery, because the broker can't tell a crashed consumer from one that processed but didn't ack. So consumers are idempotent: a processed-messages table keyed by event id, written in the same transaction as the state change. Separate transactions leave the gap where duplicates slip in.
questions.keyTakeaway: Store processed message ids in the same transaction as the state change they drive.

questions.question: What signals tell you a service boundary is wrong, and how do you correct boundary drift?
questions.answer: The loudest signal is lockstep releases: two services that always deploy together are one service in two costumes. Others are chatty calls, shared domain libraries, and schema changes in two databases at once. The fix is to merge them back, or redraw along data ownership. Boundaries are hypotheses.
questions.keyTakeaway: Lockstep releases mean the boundary is wrong; redraw along data ownership, and merging back is allowed.

questions.question: How do you design saga compensations for steps that cannot be undone, like shipping a package or sending an email?
questions.answer: I classify each step as compensatable, pivot or retriable. The pivot is the point of no return, so I push it late and put risky work before it. Past it, I retry instead of compensating, as with shipping. Where I can, I prevent: pre-authorize the card and reserve stock rather than decrement it.
questions.keyTakeaway: Put the point of no return last: compensate before the pivot, retry relentlessly after it.

questions.question: How do you set timeouts and resource limits so one slow dependency cannot take down a whole request path?
questions.answer: I start from an end-to-end budget and hand fractions down the chain, so each inner timeout is smaller than its caller's, or you get abandoned work. Bulkheads give each dependency a bounded pool, so a hung inventory service can't eat the payments threads. I prove it in load tests by hanging one on purpose.
questions.keyTakeaway: Give each hop a slice of one end-to-end budget, and give each dependency its own bulkhead.

questions.question: Is a service mesh worth adopting, and at what point does the math tip in its favor?
questions.answer: A mesh moves retries, timeouts, mTLS and telemetry into central sidecars. It's worth it with dozens of polyglot services needing uniform security. The costs are an extra hop, sidecar resources, and one more layer to debug. My threshold is ten-plus services across teams or mTLS compliance. Below that, a client library is cheaper.
questions.keyTakeaway: A mesh pays off with many polyglot services and a uniform mTLS need; below that, libraries are cheaper.

questions.question: How do you manage configuration and secrets when you have forty services across several environments?
questions.answer: I layer it: defaults baked into the image, environment values injected at deploy from a versioned store in git, and secrets pulled at runtime from Vault or a cloud key manager. Never committed, never plain env files. Short-lived tokens or workload identity mean leaks expire, and services fail fast on missing config.
questions.keyTakeaway: Defaults in the image, environment values in git, secrets short-lived in a vault; nothing hand-edited.

code.snippet:
env:
  - name: DB_HOST
    valueFrom:
      configMapKeyRef: { name: orders-config, key: host }
  - name: DB_PASSWORD
    valueFrom:
      secretKeyRef: { name: orders-db, key: password }

rows.label: Environment values
rows.note: versioned in git, injected at deploy

rows.note: pulled at runtime from a vault

questions.question: How do you choose between canary and blue-green deployments when you operate dozens of services?
questions.answer: Blue-green flips all traffic between two environments, giving instant rollback but double capacity and no gradual testing. Canary sends one to five percent of real traffic to the new version and ramps while metrics stay healthy. At scale I default to canary because it measures risk per release, and use blue-green where partial traffic is meaningless.
questions.keyTakeaway: Canary by default at scale for measured risk; blue-green where partial traffic is meaningless.

questions.question: How should team structure influence how you split services?
questions.answer: Conway's law says boundaries mirror communication. So I start with stream-aligned teams, each owning related services end to end, code to on-call. A team should build, deploy and operate without meetings. If every change needs a cross-team meeting, the boundary is wrong or a platform is missing.
questions.keyTakeaway: Split services so each team owns its services end to end with minimal cross-team coordination.

questions.question: What are your options for getting another service's data into yours, and how do you pick?
questions.answer: Four options: fetch on demand, fetch plus cache, an event-fed local read model, or CDC on the owner's DB log. Fetch is simplest and fresh but couples uptime. Event replication gives independence at the cost of lag and projection code. CDC suits legacy databases, but it leaks the schema, so I wrap it in a contract.
questions.keyTakeaway: Pick per use case: fetch for freshness, event replication for independence, CDC for legacy databases.

questions.question: When would you reach for a durable execution engine like Temporal instead of hand-rolling orchestration code?
questions.answer: Hand-rolled orchestration means owning state persistence, retries, timers and crash recovery. A durable engine like Temporal records each step, and after a crash replays history and resumes. I use one for long or money-touching workflows like multi-day fulfillment. The costs are a runtime to operate and determinism constraints. For request-scoped logic, no.
questions.keyTakeaway: Let a durable engine own workflow state, retries, and resume; hand-roll only the simplest flows.
